title: Model vetting navigation & decision lab — Halo Corp
summary: Redwood demo focused on model catalog navigation, compatibility matrix interpretation, and bench selection workflow for Halo Corp's multilingual assistant. Discussed latency vs cost tradeoffs, private vs dedicated deployment, and next steps to run a 2-week shortlist bench with KV-cache + quantization profile. Action items captured for bench config and security doc share.
topics: Deployment options: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private
Next steps for pilot and security review
action_items: Jared Park: Share bench template and test prompts (due 2026-10-22)
Maya Singh: Spin up sample bench on public test stack and share results link (due 2026-10-26)
Tom Brenner: Provide expected QPS and typical context lengths (due 2026-10-21)
Ibrahim Khalid: Confirm compliance requirements / data residency constraints (due 2026-10-23)
next_steps: Redwood to send shortlist bench template + pricing ranges
Customer to return workload profile + sample prompts
Security pack (SOC2 + network options) to be shared by Redwood)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-19 16:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Jared (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Owen (Redwood Product), Lena (Halo ML Eng), Tom (Halo Platform), Ibrahim (Halo CTO), Sara (Halo SRE)

[00:00] Jared: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, appreciate you carving out time. Quick roll call — can you all hear me okay?
[00:06] Lena: Yep loud and clear.
[00:08] Tom: Got you.
[00:10] Jared: Great. So today Maya and I will walk through how the Redwood model catalog can help you pick a small shortlist for your assistant — you mentioned multilingual support and low-cost latency targets in the pre-call notes, right Tom?
[00:22] Tom: Yeah, our goal is under 200ms p99 for short prompts at about 40 qps, cost target is, uh, basically half what we're paying right now to our managed provider. We also have some on-prem constraints for EU data.
[00:36] Maya: Ok, perfect. We'll demo the catalog filters, the compatibility matrix, and then a bench selection workflow in the console — and then show how Optimize suggests batching and quantization profiles. 
[00:47] Ibrahim: Quick thing — we need to know what private deployment options look like. If we can't go hosted with EU residency, can Redwood run in our VPC or on-prem?
[00:56] Owen: Short answer — yes. We have Redwood Private options for VPC and an on-prem package. We'll share the network diagrams in the security pack after this.
[01:05] Lena: Cool. Let's jump in.

[01:12] Maya: Alright, opening the console — you'll see the catalog landing page. First step is to set filters: language families, sequence length distributions, and latency target. Note how the UI shows model footprints and kernel compatibility.
[01:27] [screen share noise]
[01:31] Maya: I'm going to filter for multilingual models — you can see a set of open models here, both FP16 and int4 quantized variants are present. The compatibility matrix to the right maps each model to hardware targets — A100, H100, 80GB, 40GB, plus some inferred M series entries for inference-friendly kernels.
[01:49] Lena: The matrix is handy — but how reliable is that mapping? In our past experience the matrix overpromises for context length.
[01:58] Maya: Good call. The matrix is generated from our runtime profiling — we run representative sequences and kernel mapping. That said, it's heuristic: for long-context models the profile is conservative. We also show expected memory per-token and a conservative batch size recommendation.
[02:12] Sara: Is KV cache accounted for in those numbers? We rely heavily on KV cache for multi-turn.
[02:18] Maya: Yes, we surface KV cache footprint. There's a toggle to include prefix caching in the estimate. Quick note: sometimes the transcript label shows it as "cov cache" in earlier exports, we had that in QA.
[02:28] [laughter]

[02:33] Jared: Let's pick a couple of candidate models — one base open model that's cheap and one that gives higher quality for longer contexts. I'm going to add 'OpenNLP-XXL' (note: example name) and 'Polyglot-13B' to a shortlist.
[02:45] Tom: Are those names Redwood curated or community models? We need clarity for licensing.
[02:51] Maya: They're community open models we vet — each entry links to the license and known legal restrictions. We also tag models that are recommended to run with specific quant profiles to avoid hallucination regressions we've seen with aggressive quant.
[03:05] Ibrahim: How do you benchmark for quality? We need to compare multilingual BLEU-ish scores and some task specific scoring.
[03:12] Maya: We support custom eval suites — you can upload a prompt set and reference outputs. Our bench runner runs microbenchmarks (latency/p95/p99) and quality evals across your prompt set. The results come back as a matrix so you can weigh quality vs token cost.
[03:26] Lena: We have a 500-sample prompt set in Spanish + Portuguese. Would that integrate?
[03:31] Maya: Absolutely. Send the CSV or link to the S3 bucket and we'll run it in the sandbox bench.

[03:37] [05:00 — rough jump, discussion of bench config]
[05:02] Maya: For your throughput we recommend trying both int8 and int4 quant profiles. Optimize will surface an estimated cost delta and expected latency change. Note: int4 sometimes increases hallucinations for certain decoders, so we run quality checks as part of the bench.
[05:19] Lena: What's the suggested sequence length for the bench? Our typical user context is 512 tokens with a 256 token response.
[05:26] Maya: We'll set bench sequences to 768 total to be safe. Also run a short-run with 2048 for edge cases.

[05:33] Tom: On the routing side — can we set policies so short prompts hit a cheaper model while longer ones route to the high quality variant?
[05:41] Maya: Yep. Smart routing supports request-based policies: route by token-length, latency SLO, or even customer tier. You can define fallbacks — e.g., if dedicated pool is saturated, route to hosted fallback with a different model. We also demoed automatic fallback during maintenance windows.
[05:58] Ibrahim: Any gotchas for token accounting with streaming? We stream on our product; we need accurate token-costing.
[06:06] Owen: Streaming counts are the same unit as our per-token billing. We include partial tokens and have a token-level cost breakdown in the Console's trace view.

[06:15] [06:30 — Maya shows the bench runner UI]
[06:32] Maya: Here's the bench plan: baseline run, quality eval, and a multi-config sweep — different batch sizes, quant levels, and kernel maps. You can also pin runtime flags to emulate Dedicated environment (fixed GPUs, enforced KV cache).
[06:47] Lena: How do you emulate a Dedicated pool in the sandbox? We need to know if these bench numbers will match production.
[06:53] Maya: We have deterministic kernel selection and we isolate GPUs for the bench to mirror Dedicated. For absolute production parity we recommend a short dedicated pilot (72 hours) — but the bench gives a good directional signal.

[07:05] Tom: Cost modeling — show me how Optimize suggests batching size.
[07:10] Maya: Sure — Optimize ingests your latency SLO and sequence distribution. For example, at 40 qps and 200ms p99, Optimize suggested a batch size of 8 for the Polyglot-13B int8 profile on H100-80GB, which reduced token cost by ~28% with a small p99 increase of 10ms.
[07:30] Lena: That 10ms is acceptable. How confident are you in the cost delta?
[07:34] Maya: We provide confidence bands based on historical runs. For new model+quant combos the band is wider; once you run two or three benches the estimate tightens.

[07:44] [08:00 — question about security/compliance]
[08:02] Ibrahim: Walk me through audit logs and KMS. We require HSM-backed key management and immutable audit trails.
[08:10] Owen: Redwood Private supports KMS integrations (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, and HSM via partner configs). Audit logs are exportable and we can pipe them to your SIEM. We'll attach the SOC2 report and the network topology diagram.
[08:26] Sara: Do logs contain raw prompts? We prefer redaction.
[08:30] Owen: By default logs include metadata; you can configure redaction of PII or full prompt suppression. For debugging you can enable ephemeral trace dumps with strict access controls.

[08:41] [09:00 — brief cross talk about procurement]
[09:04] Ibrahim: Licensing again — if a model is under a license that requires attribution, how do you enforce that?
[09:10] Maya: We flag licenses and have a policy engine that can exclude models automatically if the license is incompatible with your product. These are surfaced in the model detail page.

[09:18] Jared: Ok, let's start a live bench. Maya — can you kick off a short 2-model sweep: OpenNLP-XXL int8 vs Polyglot-13B int8 on an H100-80GB profile, 500 example prompts (multilingual), and track quality + latency?
[09:33] Maya: Kicking it off now — submitting job. You'll get a results link in about 30–45 minutes depending on queue. For this account I'll run it in a sandbox cluster so it doesn't interfere with other runs.
[09:45] Tom: Perfect. Can you also include a run where we enable KV cache persistent hits to simulate multi-turn?
[09:52] Maya: Adding that to the job config.

[10:00] [10:15 — minor audio break, transcript artifact shows "Speaker 3" lines]
[10:20] Speaker 3: uh-huh, okay.

[10:24] Jared: While it's running, quick pricing illustration — hosted per-token ranges vs reserved dedicated pools. For a bench like this at our suggested batch and int8, projected token cost looked like roughly $0.0009/token on hosted, and with a 12-month reserved commit it's about 35% less depending on commit level.
[10:44] Tom: That's in the ballpark. We'll need a modeled ramp to present to finance.
[10:49] Jared: We'll send a pro forma with three ramp scenarios.

[10:53] Lena: One more question — how do you handle model updates/rollouts? We can't break users when a model changes behavior.
[10:59] Maya: Rollouts are controlled — canary percent, compare eval sets pre/post-deploy, automatic rollback on quality regression. We also support pinning by customer so you can keep a version until you're ready to flip.

[11:10] Ibrahim: Great. Any final open concerns from Halo side?
[11:15] Tom: Need the bench template and the security docs. Also SSO/SAML setup details for team access.
[11:22] Jared: Got it — action items noted. We'll email the bench template now and attach SOC2 + network diagram.

[11:28] Sara: Thanks, that was useful.
[11:30] Jared: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with a 30-minute pilot kickoff next week once you send the prompt set.
[11:37] Lena: Sounds good.
[11:40] [11:47 — meeting end]

Note: Transcript has occasional mislabels and minor stutters; speaker attribution may be imperfect in some timestamps.
